summary:
The national police are the documented source of the most serious risk. In September 2017 officers in Baku detained at least 100 people in raids presented as action against prostitution; detainees were beaten, interrogated, subjected to forced medical examinations and blackmailed. A United States State Department report on the period recorded threats of rape and the use of electric shocks. At least 60 of those held were imprisoned or fined. The arrests formed part of a wave of detentions ahead of the Islamic Solidarity Games, and Human Rights Watch called for an investigation and for releases. Azerbaijan acknowledged the cases in 2019, and in April 2024 the European Court of Human Rights issued a ruling on the arrests and the mistreatment.

Enforcement of this kind did not end with those arrests. In July 2023 officers raided a private birthday party in Baku; queer guests were subjected to forced medical examinations, physical and sexual harassment, and threats that their sexual orientation or gender identity would be disclosed.

Killings of trans people are documented and the response to them is inadequate. A trans woman was murdered in Baku in March 2024, and the police investigation that followed is described by monitoring organisations as inadequate. The sources available do not give Azerbaijan's general homicide rate, so this killing cannot be measured against the background rate of violence in the country; a single documented case, not a rate, is what the sources support.

Hostility in state-aligned media is routine. After a Women's Day march in 2024 whose demands included access to trans healthcare, the state-affiliated broadcaster Real TV aired discriminatory hate speech against LGBTI people. Monitoring by QueeRadar found that 77 per cent of 428 media items analysed were hateful or biased against LGBTIQ people. In a separate incident an activist was told to remove a rainbow flag in a Baku cafe. The 2017 United States State Department report recorded interference with expression, assembly and association through intimidation, incarceration on questionable charges and the blocking of websites.

Legal recognition is absent for trans people and for couples read as same-sex. Transgender people cannot change their gender entry on official documents, although they may change their name to accord with their gender identity. Marriage and civil unions between partners of the same sex are neither recognised nor performed, and same-sex couples may not adopt children, so a trans visitor whose relationship would be classified locally as a same-sex relationship has no route to recognition of that relationship. Discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is not prohibited by law. The age of consent is 16 for heterosexual and homosexual sex alike.

Coercion within families is a documented pattern. A shadow report to the UN Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women, submitted by the Gender and Development Social Union, records forced marriages of lesbian, bisexual and transgender women. In a separate case a family forcibly transported an 18-year-old woman to Baku after she came out.
tangentialFactors:
International monitoring places Azerbaijan at the bottom of the regional table. ILGA-Europe has ranked it last of 49 countries in Europe every year since 2015, citing a near total absence of legal protection.

The constitution guarantees freedom of expression, and a press council established in 2003 handles complaints under a code of conduct. Diplomatic engagement on these issues is active: the Nafas LGBTI Azerbaijan Alliance holds regular talks with the EU Delegation to Azerbaijan and other European embassies about the difficulties LGBTQ people face.

The shadow report submitted to the UN Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women by the Gender and Development Social Union describes state-approved ignorance of the situation of lesbian, bisexual and transgender women, homophobia and transphobia in official and private media, and employment discrimination; the organisation serves more than 200 LBT people.
localsOnly:
Conscription applies to able-bodied men aged 18 to 35. LGBTQIA+ recruits can be declared unfit for service under provisions of the military medical examination regulations covering personality disorders and reactive psychoses and neurotic disorders, and queer conscripts frequently conceal their sexual orientation to avoid dedovshchina hazing.

Discrimination carries direct economic costs for trans residents. An OC Media investigation found that trans people are rejected from jobs and housing and pushed into black-market work and precarious housing. It profiles Durdana, 29, who was arrested, denied housing and employment, and became dependent on community support after her trans-friendly employer closed.

Community infrastructure is thin but present. The Gender Resource Center (Gender Resurs Mərkəzi), established in 2020, is a queer-feminist platform created in response to the lack of safe space and resources for people of different genders and sexual orientations. Gender and Development, created in 2007, runs local projects in collaboration with the Ministry of Health. AZAD LGBT ran in-person programming in Baku, including LGBTQ film nights attended by a local psychologist who joined post-screening discussions, and launched a website in 2015 providing free online LGBTQ education tools; Minority Magazine also covers education topics. Community media date to gay.az, launched on 25 May 2011 by Ruslan Balukhin, and Minority Magazine, founded by Samad Ismayilov in December 2015 and registered as an NGO from August 2017. A documentary by Ismayilov about a trans man premiered in Baku on 25 November 2017 with Dutch embassy support before an audience of about 80 people.

Schools have produced the one documented enforcement response in this area. In April 2019 a 14-year-old pupil in Baku attempted suicide after homophobic bullying at school; the principal took no action, attributed the attempt to family difficulties and did not call an ambulance, and the pupil died in hospital two days later. The school director, deputy director and psychologist were dismissed, and on 24 October 2019 the Sabail District Court of Baku sentenced the principal to 2 years and 2.5 months of restricted liberty plus 18,500 AZN (about $10,882) in compensation. The case prompted a nationwide social media campaign and a Ministry of Education anti-bullying action plan launched on 13 May 2019 with a new hotline, intended to ensure a healthy environment in general education institutions, improve school-family relations and protect students from abuse.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources in this inventory carry no detail on entry rules, visa processing or airport and border screening for trans travellers arriving in Azerbaijan, and nothing on how travel documents or prosthetics would be handled at a port of entry.

The April 2024 European Court of Human Rights ruling on the 2017 arrests is recorded as issued; the sources available do not set out its terms or what compliance has followed.

Whether the press council established in 2003 has assessed complaints that state-controlled media used homosexuality to discredit government critics is not known.

A Women's Day march in 2024 demanded access to trans healthcare, which indicates that such access is contested, but the inventory contains no detail on whether gender-affirming care is legally available in Azerbaijan or how a visitor would obtain it.
